reviews.transcript_full: [Music] Welcome back. In this video, we're stepping on board Delta Airlines in business class aboard an Airbus A330 flying from Madrid, Spain to Atlanta, Georgia in the USA. Is this old and dated Delta 1 cabin worth the hefty price tag? Stay tuned to find out why Delta's recent retrofit of this aircraft missed the mark. We'll also tell you what you need to look for if you're looking to book Delta's business class product in order to make sure you know what you're booking before you board. So, join us as we explore the seat, service, and experience on board this 9 and 1/2 hour daytime flight. And stick around to learn about Delta's plans for these aircraft. Welcome to Travel at Random. We're Trevor and Ryan. This channel started out of a love of travel. We're here to share unbiased and self-funded trip reports, hotel and flight reviews, and travel advice. We hope we inspire your next getaway. Check out our playlist in the description and browse the channel. If you enjoy this video, please hit that like button and subscribe to keep up with our latest content. Thank you for watching. Now, let's head to the airport. [Applause] [Music] Welcome to Madrid, the capital of Spain. We are just wrapping up a week of exploring several historic Spanish cities. Check out our playlist at the end of the video to see more from our trip. We'll have new videos in this series over the next few months, so make sure you subscribe to stay uptodate. Today we're flying Delta out of Adulo Suarez Madrid Barahas International Airport, Barahas or MAD for short. Last year over 66 million passengers made their way through this airport, making it one of the busiest in Europe. MAD is located about 7 mi or 11 km from the city center, about 15 minutes by train or 30 minutes by car or taxi. The airport is connected to Madrid's public transit. Metro line 8 has stops at all four terminals and the commuter train system has a train station at terminal 4. There are five terminals in total. Terminals 1, 2, and three are older and are connected. Terminal 4 and 4S are newer and about 5 km from the other terminals. You can take a shuttle to move between 4, 4S, and the older terminals. Delta operates out of terminal 1 along with most of the other major international carriers. Except for one world alliance members like Iberia and American Airlines which are out of terminal 4. We're traveling in Delta 1 today. So there's a dedicated baggage drop and check-in line just for business class passengers. If you're flying Delta, enter through door 1 at terminal 1 and head to the right. Just look for the Delta 1 sign. Check-in was rather quick and we were off to security and passport control. There is fasttrack security at this airport and it was included with the Delta 1 ticket. The passport control line was pretty quick at this time of the morning and we were through in a few minutes. As part of your Delta 1 ticket, you also have access to the Seless VIP lounge which is located near gate B29 up the escalators just past the duty-free shop. This is also a priority pass lounge and is the only lounge in terminal 1. There are no Delta or Sky Team specific lounges in this airport. The Seless Lounge is large and there was plenty of seating available the morning of our flight. Most seats are set up at tables. This club also features a large outdoor terrace that wraps around the building, offering 180° views of the runway, remote stands, and gates. [Music] There are a lot of seating options out here, including some elevated sections with sofas. In the center was the main food and drink buffet. For breakfast, it had pastries, fruits, cold cuts, and salad items available. [Music] On the back wall are pairs of grabandgo refrigerators with items like packaged sandwiches, fruit cups, and bottled drinks. [Music] In the middle are two self-service espresso style drink machines. On the far side of the lounge is a large bar with wine, cocktails, soda, and beer on offer, even at 8:00 a.m. The club had showers available, which you can request. Since we were leaving first thing in the morning and we came from our hotel, we skipped the showers. The lounge also has pretty nice and clean bathrooms. Near the entrance, there's a quiet room with some tables where you can get some work done. Reviews online of this lounge are mixed with some reporting long entry lines and picked over food offerings. As far as lines go, there's always a customer arguing about access at any club we go to these days. But there were multiple agents working it, so it was less than five minutes. The food on offer looked fine, but was pretty basic for breakfast with the only hot option being a toaster for the bread. Overall, the lounge was a nice space to spend a little bit of time and grab a drink. The terrace was unexpected, and we always appreciate being able to get some fresh air while traveling. Otherwise, it's a pretty standard international priority pass lounge. Our daytime flight today takes us 9 and a half hours from MAD to ATL, about 4,300 miles. Delta flies this route once daily. Boarding started on time and was orderly. There were clearly marked cues for each zone. After scanning our boarding passes, we were surprised to be heading down some stairs. [Music] We then found out that we were on a remote stand this morning. This caused the actual boarding to be a bit chaotic as they loaded several zones into the bus before sending it off and everyone rushed the single set of air stairs at the same time. This Airbus A330300 features 282 seats across four classes. 34 Delta 1 seats, 21 premium select seats, 24 comfort plus seats, and 208 economy seats. Delta 1 seats on this A330 are arranged in a one 121 reverse herring bone configuration. We're in seats 2A and 2J today. The bulkhead on opposite sides of the plane. Privacy was reasonable, but mainly due to having your back facing the aisle, not due to the walls of the seat. Be aware, these are not Delta's newer suites, and the seats do not feature closing doors. If a door is important to you, make sure you look for flights operated by Delta's A350s and A330900 Neos. When booking, look at the more details to see the aircraft type. Delta 767s have a variant of the Delta 1 suite, but don't feature closing doors due to the narrower cabin width. Delta will also eventually have closing door suites on their upcoming A321 Neos that feature Delta 1. These A330 Delta 1 cabin seats are 19.6 7 in wide and are fully lie flat. There was plenty of room to lay down, even for Trevor at 6'4. [Music] Each seat features a 15.4 in touchscreen if that swings out, as well as USBA and universal power outlets. The tray table extends from the side console and folds open. It's a good size for both dining and getting some work done. While in seat mode, the seat has great leg room. I'm 6 foot for reference. There's also an adjustable armrest on the aisle side. Delta's A33300's underwent interior refits in 2021. In 2022, a new premium select cabin with 21 seats in a 232 configuration were added. The Comfort Plus cabin was downsized from 40 to 24 seats in a 242 arrangement. They also refreshed the lavatories and even added an espresso machine. Delta 1 and economy cabins got new upholstery, but otherwise went unchanged. These current seats are rather dated and are not as private or modern as Delta's other widebody Delta 1 seats. Delta must agree because they've announced they're going to refit these aircraft in 2026. They plan to start taking the 42 aircraft back into refit to replace the business class cabin with the latest Delta 1 seats. Each seat had a Mason branded bedding pack that includes a pretty substantial pillow and a good quality duvet. This flight also featured Delta's brand new mattress toppers which are now available on all Delta 1 flights. At this seat were also noiseancelling headphones, a large bottle of water, and an amenity kit. Delta's current amenity kit is from a Sony. It has a dark blue soft leatherrett bag with a zipper and contains a small card for the brand, an eye mask, and some of the nicest airplane socks we've seen. Normally, these things are like tissue paper, but these were decidedly thick and even had a nice Delta logo on the back. Rounding out the kit are earplugs, Grown Alchemist brand hand cream and lip balm, a dental kit, and a cardboard pen. Prior to departure, we were served a welcome drink. The standard sparkling wine, orange juice, or a mimosa. We had a lengthy taxi this morning to get out to the runway, but once we were there, we were off. [Music] [Applause] There have been a number of wildfires in Spain this summer, so the skies are a little bit hazy. [Music] Now that we're up in the air, let's take a look at the onboard entertainment. One area where these seats really show their age is the if system. The screen swings out when you push a button to release it from the seat in front of you. My screen was not very bright, and the touch is not responsive. There is a remote, but in our experience, it takes a little getting used to, as the arrows work almost 90 degrees to what you would expect. The selection of movies and TV shows was similar to older Delta planes and was decent, but the more modern IF systems have more content. The flight tracker and moving map are almost completely useless and show just how much better the newer systems are on other aircraft. Just look at this graphic. As mentioned earlier, the seats also have a universal power outlet near your shoulder, and there's a USB port. These aircraft are also equipped with Wi-Fi, which is free for all Sky Miles members in all cabins. It worked fairly well and was relatively consistent across the flight. Shortly after takeoff, the flight attendants were up and hard at work. Service started with a hot towel, followed by a drink service, and nuts. Trevor and I both opted for a glass of the Bordeaux red wine. It was decent. However, in our experience, the red wines in Delta 1 aren't very premium. Delta does also offer real champagne in Delta 1. Delta allows you to pre-order your meal a week ahead of the flight. Here's a look at the menu for today's route. I opted for the seafood paella and Trevor ordered the duck.com fee. [Music] following drinks and nuts, the starters arrived. The starter was a Thai coconut curry soup, chilled shrimp with herb crimp fish, a garden salad with roasted tomatoes, and a warm roll. The salad was actually the best part. The shrimp were good and tender, but we think the version with the aioli on some other routes is better. The soup was pretty good, but would have benefited from a little bit more curry flavor. The crew then moved on to mains. Their service was friendly and efficient on this flight. One thing to keep in mind is that the galley for Delta 1 on these A330s is at the back of the cabin, so they served rear to front. The paella included fish and shrimp. The fish was moist and not overcooked. The shrimp were also well prepared. The dish was a good take on paella, but after a few days in Valencia on this trip, not terribly authentic. The duckcomb feet came with spiced poached pears, carrots, kale, and mashed potatoes. The dish overall was good, but a little bland. The sauce didn't have much flavor, but when all mixed together, it was decent. It was nice to have the fresh veggies, which were well cooked and still had some texture, which is nice, and it wasn't overly heavy. The duck was shredded and served as sort of a ball wrapped in the skin. The duck was a little dry, and there was a tiny bone fragment, so this was a miss, we'd say. For dessert, the options were fruit and cheese, ice cream sundaes, or a Sarrento lemon cake. I opted for the ice cream. Trevor had the lemon cake. The cake was a dome of whipped cream with a thin slice of cake with lemon filling and coated with a thin layer of chocolate. This was light, fresh, and enjoyable. The entire main meal service was completed about 2 hours after departure. During the flight, the crew made themselves available for drink refills. They set up snacks and bottled water in the forward galley, and passengers were welcome to help themselves. Mid-flight, the crew baked cookies. This is one of our favorite features of Delta 1, and the flight attendants often take pride in the fresh baked chocolate chip cookies at 36,000 ft. During the flight, we came down the East Coast and had some great views in New York. About 90 minutes before arrival, the crew came around with a hot snack. The options were a pizza or a cheeseburger. I opted for the burger and requested the cheese be removed before they heated it up, and the person was happy to oblige. I made this request earlier in the flight since I don't eat cheese. Trevor was offered a tomato and basil pizza. They had run out of the burger by the time they reached midc cabin. He reported that the pizza was actually really good. The crust was crisp and soft, not soggy at all. The pizza came with roasted vegetables and pesto and a very dense chocolate cake. After the snack, it was about time to descend into Atlanta. Enjoy the landing and we'll be back to wrap things up. [Music] We landed from the west and then taxied to gate F1. So that's the Delta 1 experience on the A330 from Madrid to Atlanta. While these seats are definitely not as private as some of Delta's newer seats, the flight was comfortable and the crew was great. While old, the seats are definitely spacious. Delta excels at the soft product with a friendly and responsive crew and decent food. The hard product is inconsistent. Delta has too many aircraft with different Delta 1 seats, but they are working to bring the fleet closer to alignment. These A330s are some of the oldest business class seats in Delta's lineup, but that should start to disappear next year. To recall a bit, if you want to fly Delta's latest product, look for the A330 900 Neo or A350 aircraft. You'll also find upgraded Delta 1 seats on the 767s. They just won't have closing doors. A few months ago, we flew Delta 1 to Lima, Peru on an Airbus A350. We'll link that review down in the description. That plane had a unique configuration that's about to disappear. Also, make sure you check out our entire Spain playlist. We'll be releasing new content over the next few months, including hotel reviews, city tours, and Spain by highspeed rail. If you enjoy this video, please give it a thumbs up and make sure you subscribe to keep up with our latest content. Both of these are a great way you can help out the channel. We really appreciate it. Thank you for watching. We'll see you on the next adventure.

a little bit of wear and tear is understandable. Greetings in English and Chinese (Cantonese & Putonghua)
Flight time would be 11h47m The space in front looked barely enough to walk
and would probably bother the passenger. Not so aisle-access as I thought Printed menu was distributed by FA Baked chicken fried rice, Braised beef or vegeterian choice
Mushroom and spinach risotto. Shortly after safety demo, we were ready to depart Cloudy morning, very Manchester Here we go A bottled water was distributed shortly after take off Followed by nuts and drink service (12:05pm) I planned to watch three live Premier League games The live streaming is smooth and clear I really enjoyed it becaues the flight departed at 10:30am UK time,
I did not feel sleepy at all. Lunch was served from the front compartment to the back
I chose the baked chicken rice. (1:16pm) It tasted surprisingly good although the serving may be
a little bit small for lunch if I didn't have my breakfast Always love the view from the window Nice sunset near Georgia After the second game, walk to galley to stretch my legs
Snacks in the galley Hot noodle was my choice. I am quite sure it was customised, s
mell not as strong as those purchased from supermarkets. Another concern of these exit row seats are their
proximity to the toilets This seat is ok, but I think row 59 may feel it a bit bothersome. Cannot sleep at all, can only enjoy the night view from sky. 05:50am HKT, breakfast was served
Also from the front compartment to the back Congee with 2 prawns, not bad 06:23 HKT descending to Hong Kong International Airport
Here are some final thoughts CX Airbus A350 economy class is good
at least better than its 777-300er in 3-4-3 seating config The extra legroom seat 60A/K is ok
Can walk from the narrow space in front But if you wish to walk around quite often, aisle seats
or row 59 seats are better choices Because going in and out would inevitably 
bother the passenger in front In terms of the best seat in economy class on CX A350-900, 
I would prefer bulkhead seats in row 40A/C/H/K. I sat at seat 40C on my return flight, and the passengers at 40A/B
did not have to wake me in order to walk out from their seats Lounge 1903 at Manchester Airport T2 is good I like the made-to-order toast and Cheshire Farm ice cream so much There could be more snacks available in the galley
and it would be better if water and juice were ready to take In-flight entertainment system is superb! I enjoy the 3 premier league games on this flight  No free wifi in economy class unless you are CX Diamond member Hope free wifi will become norm in the future You always need some luck to have a cry-free flight, 
but this time, I didn't. Price. About GBP 800 for a MAN-HKG return ticket
Direct flight is more expensive than that with transfer. For comparison, my wife's PEY ticket with AF & KLM also costed her
around GBP 800, but only with 2 carry-on luggages. Find the best deal is better than stick to any specific airlines IMO. Thank you for watching and I will soon post another video
comparing this extra legroom seat and 40A/K bulkhead seats. Stay tuned!

reviews.transcript_full: in-flight entertainment or ife is one of the more exciting parts of long-haul travel with most airlines installing screens on wide-body aircraft depending on the airline you fly with ife can vary in the selection and quality of content but how exactly do the entertainment systems work are they on their way out due to cost reduction well let's find out [Music] while in-flight entertainment might feel like a given on modern long-haul planes on most carriers the technology itself is newer than you might think you may have noticed that some older planes still have drop down screens from the overhead panel these screens were original ifv systems with screens playing a single movie at a time passengers could individually plug in earphones and listen to the movie on the screen individual screens one heard off until the late 1980s where northwest airlines ran a test of a 2.7 inch in-seat display on the 747 the airline received overwhelming support for this video on demand system and this sparked the ife screen trend that we see today however drop-down screens remained in service until the early 2000s with some airlines until they were gradually phased out nowadays most airlines come with large in-seat displays that offer a variety of content but how does this work well ife systems seemingly work without any visible wires the wiring is actually tucked away into the aircraft walls with the wiring starting in the top panel next to the oxygen masks and ac vents these wires then connect to the power units which are present every few rows in the side wall of the aircraft some small avionic systems are also present under the seat completing the entire system these days modern ife units don't use too much wiring allowing a few fiber optic cables to carry much the data and power this means the entire system is a lot lighter and streamlines now than before where passengers routinely found large ife boxes blocking their somewhat limited legroom the installation of ife units happens along with the seats when the plane is nearing completion this allows teams to install the system and then cover up any visible wires under the interior of the cabin the reducing weight of these systems have allowed airlines to install more of these without spending billions on the project however retrofitting an aircraft cabin with ife screens can still cost over 3 million dollars per aircraft and it costs a fuel to operate each screen only adding to the price so what about content well ife screens are exciting the system is only as good as the content available this is where the individual airlines come into play depending on how much they're willing to pay airlines could invest in new releases which cost them pay per view or older content according to a report from the valor consultancy in-flight movies are divided into early window content and late window content and international movies the early window content are the most expensive and feature movies that have just left theaters late window content includes all older movies which includes classics and other tent to be popular and much cheaper for the airlines international movies tend to be the cheapest and more region specific with the fewer options usually available except the carrier's home country usually negotiate content prices with hollywood studios directly with the price depending on the route being flown and the box office ratings of the movie in question for other movies airlines could just purchase the movies for a flat yearly licensing fee the airline movie business is a big one with the estimated market to be 425 million dollars last year additional content includes music video games a 3d moving map and more options while these do all add to the cost movies still make up the bulk of the expenditure but ife screens are going out of fashion while passengers may enjoy content on their seat back airlines are slowly realizing that it's far too expensive to maintain the additional weight of these systems the power needed to run them and the cost of movies and screens is extremely high for carriers instead airlines are slowly moving towards a new system stream content directly to your device with most passengers now flying having access to a phone laptop or tablet it's much cheaper for the airlines to ditch the bulky system and install in-flight wi-fi instead contents can then be streamed directly to those devices cutting costs for airlines while this can drain the device's battery for planes or power plants this isn't a major issue now then the future while this year of 2020 and 21 downturn has affected most innovations in the in-flight entertainment department with airlines focusing on reducing services there is still a broad future for this market the growing prevalence of in-flight wi-fi allows for services like netflix amazon prime video and more to become accessible over the air shaking up the entire system as we know it most new generation wide bodies are also wi-fi ready requiring little additional work to activate the systems in-flight entertainment is an integral part of the flying experience now with reviews.transcript_full: This is Level Airlines and I'm going to share my experience on board this low-cost carrier.  If you are flying on level, you're likely going to want to temper your expectations.  Don't expect much. It's really no frills and that's what you should expect if you're going to book a ticket on here.  It's very easy to think you're buying a ticket on Iberia Airlines only to find out that your code shared on level.  Believe it or not, the best part of the level experience is their seat back entertainment.  The screens in the back of the seat are large, responsive and new.  I've been on plenty of traditional airlines who see back entertainment either it doesn't exist or is antiquated.  Now that is probably where my praise of level airlines will stop.  There's not much beyond that. Okay.  The aircraft that we flew on level was a 333 configuration. That meant it was pretty tight.  The seats left little legroom. As you can see here, my knees were budding up against the seat in front of me the entire flight.  Now, if this was a short-haul trip, that really wouldn't be a problem.  This flight, however, was a transatlantic flight. So I was in this position for about seven hours.  The only thing I could imagine that would be worse than where I was on this seat would be the middle of the middle aisle.  That would be tough. No food or soft drinks were included at all.  But that's expected for a low-cost carrier. You could, however, buy snacks.  So you'd absolutely be better off bringing your own snacks as opposed to buying these on board.  So let me know what you think about level airlines. Have you been on? If you have, drop a comment about your experience below.  Thanks again for watching and we'll see you next time.

reviews.transcript_full: There are often a few things we can enjoy to pass the time while crossing the world at subsonic speeds over 30,000 ft above sea level on a commercial airliner. On the long flights, after enjoying a meal and drinks, we then decide what we want to do for the rest of the time. Some will take a short nap or just go to sleep or start to read a book or magazine. Those sitting in the window seats can enjoy the window views. Then there's the option to watch a movie or listen to music on the seatback screen or our own device. Since the first commercial flights, keeping passengers occupied while infight has been a question airline operators have asked themselves. One answer has been to provide audio and video systems referred to as infight entertainment or if to provide content such as movies and music to enjoy while on board. Today, these systems have been advanced to allow passengers to go beyond movies and music to play video games, see outside views of the aircraft, or get the flight status and connecting flight information on their own seat. if systems have come a long way from the early projection screens to show the very first inflight movies to the vast content libraries available on HD seatback screens today. So in this video, we'll take a look at the history of inflight entertainment systems and how airlines have made improvements to these systems that not only we enjoy inflight but have empowered passengers and enhanced the overall travel experience. Far from the modern IF systems we enjoy today, the very first infight video was shown on a short fight over the skies of Chicago in the early 1920s. In the August 22, 1921 issue of Aerial Age magazine, history's first aerial movie show took place aboard an 11 seat Felixto F5 flying boat named the Santa Maria as part of Chicago's Pageant of Progress trade show. The short film shown was named Howdy Chicago, which was a local production to promote the city. According to the account on aerial age, the film was shown on a plane while flying 90 mph 2,000 ft above the city of Chicago. A dey suitcase projection machine was fastened in a position and connected with an electrical flight socket. The film was viewed on a projection screen towards the front of the cabin and it was switched on by a projectionist who pressed the button to start it. This was the first known experiment in showing a flight on board an aircraft. Though the technology at the time was limited, it was described as a success. An account from the article said, quote, "Before the flight, it was feared that the vibration of the giant hydroplane as it shot through at 90 mph would seriously interfere with the screening, but it did not." This historic flight demonstrated the practicability of movie entertainment for transatlantic aerial commuters in the days to come. The success of the film screening on the promotional flights around Chicago opened up the ideas for those in aviation and how to show films on board. This would lead to the very first featurelength movie film being shown a few years later aboard a Imperial Airways flight. On April 6th, 1925, the very first movie shown on an airplane, The Lost World, was promoted by Imperial Airways with its flights as being quote the world's first aircraft cinema. Following the first movie showings aboard the Imperial Airways flights, airlines would experiment using radio signals from the ground for live broadcasts and performances from singers. Fast forward to the 1960s and jet aircraft then started to fly faster, higher, and for longer distances than the previous generation of planes. The aviation industry had to adjust some challenges to show movies on planes, such as getting the reels on board. The other challenge was to find a projector that could withstand turbulence yet be light enough not to add extra weight onto the aircraft. These challenges would be solved by cinema owner named Dave Flexer. Flexer would start a company named Infight Motion Pictures, a company that would lead to the rise of regular film showings on flights, but also served as the foundation for systems that the aviation industry would improve on later. After an investment of $1 million, Flexer and his company would develop a 16mm film system with a 25-in reel mounted horizontally to maximize space. Passengers would view the film on a projector at the front of the cabin. Using the new system, Transorld Airways showed the movie by Love Possessed to firstclass passengers on board a Boeing 707 in 1961. TWWA's main rival Pan-American would then follow and a year later Pakistan International Airways became the first international airline to introduce inflight movies with the same new system. The ability to show films on board aircraft presented an opportunity for airlines to show another type of film before a flight inflight safety videos. Provided the aircraft had the required video and sound systems, the US FAA from 1984 allowed for these pre-recorded videos to be shown replacing the standard live demonstrations performed by flight attendants. Airlines such as TWWA, Panama, and Northwest began showing their own inflight safety videos to passengers using the onboard screens. The aviation industry would continue to experiment with new media technologies that were introduced in the 1970s and 1980s such as videotapes, closed circuit television, and overhead screens. The one airline, Northwest Airlines, would make infight entertainment become more personal with the introduction of individual seatback screens in the late 1980s. During this time, Arn Stevenson, a businessman involved in aviation components, wanted to put a small liquid crystal display LCD TV screen for each airplane seat. This would lead to the founding of a new company, Airvision, and the company would partner with Philips for the screens. Warner Brothers would provide the content for this new IF system. And in June 1988, Northwest Airlines began trials using the new IF system on its flights between Detroit and Tokyo. Airvision's if was the world's first with personal if screens. The Boeing 747 on Northwest Detroit Tokyo flights had 116 of the 6.9 cm seatback screens installed on which passengers could watch video content on six channels. These six channels showed movies, news, documentaries, music videos, and cartoons on a fixed schedule. Both Northwest and Warner Brothers surveyed the passengers, and the result was 70% preferred the personal screens to the overhead screens. Following Northwest, British Airways and Quantis would launch their own trials of Airvision's IP system on board their aircraft. From six channels offered on the Northwest Airlines 747s, these IP systems would expand with far bigger libraries and CPC screens going beyond movies and music to offer passengers the ability to play video games, listen to podcasts, watch live TV, see the inflight map, and even communicate with their fellow passengers. Among the biggest libraries of content that airline passengers can enjoy today comes from Emirates ICE system. Widely regarded as the world's largest with 6,500 channels of audio video on demand content. It is one of the well- reggarded IF systems along with Qatar Airways Orics, Singapore Airlines Chrisworld and Cafe Pacific's own system. Of the audio video on demand IF systems today, Singapore Airlines Chris World is widely regarded as the first to allow passengers to pause, rewind, and fast forward movies or music. After launching Chrisworld in 1995 with 32 audio and video channels and 10 video games, it launched the new system called Wisemen 3000 in September of 1997. First introduced to first and business class passengers, it was then rolled out to economy class passengers in 2001. In addition to the media control options, it also featured news text displays and destination information. While Chris World is the longest active prior to the Singapore's Wisemen 3000, Swiss Air had launched its own audio video on demand system earlier in the year 1997 with its own system powered by interactive flight technologies. Similar to Wisemen 3000, it also let passengers watch pay-per-view movies and take gaming on an airplane to another level with infight gambling. However, that system was cited as a factor in the crash of Swiss Air Flight 111. Prior to the crash, Swiss Air complained that the electric boxes under the seat would get too warm and hard drives installed failed regularly. Following the crash, Swiss Air removed the IFT system from aircraft with them and it was never used again. Well into the 2000s and the rise of the internet, airlines, including the budget airlines, have expanded the streaming the very same content on their IF systems beyond the seatback screen, but rather onto the passenger's very own device. This has led to the rise of the bring your own device model, providing inflight entertainment. Airlines now make decisions on whether to install seatback entertainment screens or skip it in favor of providing Wi-Fi and content through passengers own devices. To install modern seatback screens, the cost can vary depending on aircraft. Whether it's a small narrow body jet or a wide body such as the 8380, a typical individual seatback installation can cost between $10,000 to $15,000 per seat. Along with the installation of wirings, servers, power systems, insec controls, airlines also have to invest heavily in both the hardware and software along with the maintenance after installation. Combined those costs can be far higher than offering a Wi-Fi system minus the seatback screens. Adopting the bring your own device model, airlines, especially budget airlines, can focus on modifying the seats to offer maybe a device holder and charging ports. With these choices, airlines may have fleets with mixed entertainment systems. Their narrow body jets used on short hall flights may have just bring your own device systems, while widebody jets used on medium and long haul flights featuring both Wi-Fi and seatback screens. Whether aircraft are equipped with seatback screens or not, more aircraft are now featuring seatback charging ports as passengers increasingly bring their own devices on board. Passengers can also use their own audio devices such as Bluetooth enabled earphones to enjoy the content. Compared to the IF systems of the past, modern seatback and wireless systems also provide passengers more flight information. Passengers can view the current flight status information and the exact location of the aircraft on interactive maps. External cameras installed on select aircraft such as the Airbus A380, A350, and 7 intended for pilots to navigate on the ground. allows for passengers to view things that they would normally not get during takeoff and landing. In addition to getting the estimated arrival time, passengers can also access connecting flight information and airport terminal maps at key airline hubs through the same if systems. While some aircraft lets passengers enjoy external views to the IF, one airline has allowed passengers to actually listen into the conversations between the pilots and air traffic controllers United. There is no official history of Channel 9 and it's not really mentioned by the airline, though it history goes back to the 1980s. There are videos on YouTube that do feature passengers listening in onto the pilot ATC conversations on channel line, but on board the pilot in the command has the final decision on whether the passengers can listen into it. Today, it can be found on United Seatback screens listed as from the flight deck. In recent years, there has been an increased interest from airlines and the traveling public for infight Wi-Fi access. On a casual poll on the Fights in Asia X page, when asked which is more important on a flight, having infight Wi-Fi or an in-flight entertainment screen, over 70% of the over 180 people voted for the Wi-Fi. In a larger poll of over 11,000 passengers by Viasat, 81% of those surveys said that being able to connect is more important for them. Among the headline internet providers has been SpaceX's Starlink, which has seen a growing list of major airlines selecting Starlink to provide free high-speed internet access on board. Starlink is one company that addresses an interest from passengers and airlines for great internet access on board flights, which the 2023 VISAT survey also reported 48% of passengers want the reassurance of free and reliable internet on board an aircraft. Having this feature is an important and will influence booking decisions as 83% of respondents in the VISAT survey said that they would select an airline if they offered quality Wi-Fi experience. With more surveys showing similar sentiments and a growing number of airlines introducing free onboard internet, it is becoming clear having free high-speed internet access is becoming an important factor when selecting which airline to fly with. Going forward, the basic amenities most airlines will offer to each passengers will be free internet access and charging ports. Budget airlines and those with aircraft operating shorter flights will likely take the route of bring your own device, while bigger full service carriers may choose the hybrid model that allows connections between passengers devices and the seatback screen. Regardless, there are opportunities for budget and full service carriers to incorporate personal greetings and allow passengers to enhance their infight experience by using it for meal orders, showing food and beverage options, reading materials, or communicating with the flight attendants. Airlines could further experiment with technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality, but the successes of those technologies will depend heavily on the ability for passengers to enjoy these activities in the limited space on the plane. even in the premium seats and the needed equipment can safely be installed on the aircraft. That said, modern IF have come a long way from the simple projector showing how Chicago. We now have more options when it comes to the types of content and games to keep us occupied as airlines push the boundaries of flight. We are no longer just limited to the personal screen, but can enjoy and control the same content and connect to the internet on our own devices. With the internet, if systems expanded what can be enjoyed in a flight beyond the seatback screen. That's all for now, though I do want to hear your thoughts. Which airline has your favorite inflight entertainment system? As inflight Wi-Fi becomes more common, which is more important, the internet access or having an I screen? And how do you see the future of inflight entertainment? I definitely would love to hear your thoughts again, but in the meantime, this has been another edition of Flights in Asia, highlighting the news and updates from the aviation and travel scene in the Asia Pacific. Thank you for watching and have a great day.

reviews.transcript_full: reported today in the verge. United's latest jets will offer Bluetooth for inflight entertainment.  United Airlines is adding a long awaited feature to the inflight entertainment seatback  screens of its new Boeing 737 MAX-8 jets, support for Bluetooth headphones. The company is  making the upgrade as part of United Next, a new plan to expand and modernize its fleet  with what it says are larger, fuel-efficient jets and a more comfortable inflight experience.  I haven't flown in the last two years, for reasons that are hopefully obvious, but the  thing that grinds most of my past flying experience to a halt is dealing with the bizarre  Tuporong Daudi OJax airplanes used for inflight audio. Having headphones with a 3.5mm  Zordio jack isn't hard, but it doesn't reflect the Bluetooth audio lifestyle, Apple,  and plenty of other tech companies have slowly forced me to adopt. I don't like the wireless  audio freak I've become, but it happened, which makes United's upgrades so exciting,  as demoed in the tweets below from aviation writer Jason Rabinovitz. The main attraction  of it United's new interior is the new at Panasonic Caroseat Back-Eye System. It finally offers  one of the overall most requested passenger items, Bluetooth audio. Narrow-body aircraft  with these screens will finally make it a reality.  Hashtagpacsexpick.twitter.com slash TDO04G4 by 7C. Adding seatback screens made a huge  difference in how tolerable flying is, but it's been held up by lagging audio support  that the Verge has even written a guide to getting around. And this isn't a problem  unique to United. Other airlines like Delta or JetBlue have been offering seatback screens  for years, but have also saddled flyers with analog audio. United just might be one of the  first airlines to start the next wave of in-flight entertainment improvements, hopefully.  However, there's room for things to go a bit sideways. As part of its upgrades, United's  new 737 Max8 jets offer 10 or 13-inch in-flight entertainment screens on the backs of all seats,  which might mean a lot of people trying to connect to Bluetooth at once. That could cause  interference, and might also make the process of connecting your headphones more of a chore if  you're having to hunt through multiple devices trying to pair in the same menu. United currently  only offers Bluetooth on its Max8 jets which it says should start flying this summer.  The company didn't share how it plans to address issues with Bluetooth, but said it's still  studying the technology. I can't rightfully claim that Bluetooth is as meaningful a change  as more a grimoire safer flights, but for an airline industry hoarding cash to make it through  the pandemic and looking to entice frequent flyers to earn their miles again, any snazzy new feature  can't hurt.For more on this story, visit the news article link.
