reviews.transcript_full: Everyone, did you know that there is an airport right near us that once vied for the top two spots in the world for passenger volume? Unfortunately, it is not Incheon Airport, nor is it far away in Hong Kong or Singapore. Today, we are talking about an airport in China that ranked second in the world for passenger traffic before COVID-19 but has completely collapsed since the pandemic! This is a review of my flight from Beijing Capital Airport, the capital of China, to Gimpo on Korean Air. Beijing Capital Airport, also known as PEK (or Capital Airport), was one of Asia's main airports, ranking second in the world for passenger volume with over 100 million annual passengers as of 2019. Beijing Capital International Airport is also the main hub for China's flag carrier, Air China. It is likely one of the airports you have considered for a layover at least once, as Air China offers incredibly cheap flights to Europe via Beijing. However, the situation has been gradually changing since the COVID-19 pandemic. Based on Terminal 2, which Korean Air uses, the facilities had become outdated due to continuous use without major renovations since its opening in 1999. Furthermore , as demand continued to rise, the airport reached saturation, leading to the opening of a new airport south of Beijing in 2019. That place is now PKX Beijing Daxing International Airport. Recently, it seems the Chinese government and airlines are pushing for support for Daxing Airport. For starters, China Southern Airlines has moved its hub to Daxing, and only Air China and some Star Alliance airlines... They are staying at PKX while the other airlines are moving to Daxing and investing in facilities there. Even though people say Daxing is failing, it seems the trend is to inevitably push Daxing because further upgrades to the Capital Airport are impossible. Ah, but then again, the situation at Daxing doesn't seem that great either... well, I guess they will figure it out. Anyway, today I will show you my experience flying Korean Air from Beijing Capital Airport (Shoudu Airport) to Gimpo—which used to be (and still is) China's capital airport, but has become a bit of a shady hub. Korean Air is still using the Capital Airport and operates a total of four flights to the metropolitan area : three from Incheon and one from Gimpo. Oh, they do operate one flight a week from Busan on weekdays as well, but the timing is absolutely terrible. Seeing that Asiana operates similarly, I am curious whether they will transfer the eight flights to and from Seoul alone after the merger to LCCs or foreign airlines , or if they will operate all of them themselves . I came in the day before on a China Eastern domestic flight, so oh wow, this is really ... I had a flight canceled and so many other things happened ... I have a lot to say, but I'll save that for the next video. I will try to get back to it soon. Anyway, after arriving on a domestic flight, I stayed one night at the Ibis near the airport. After sleeping there, I took Didi Taxi, the Chinese version of Kakao Taxi, to the airport . It took about 10 minutes and cost around 22 yuan. If you are flying with Korean Air, you need to come to T2, or Terminal 2. For your information, North Korea's Air Koryo also uses Terminal 2. If you fly Korean Air on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday, you can see the Air Koryo counter and aircraft. I didn't go out of my way to look for them, but if you are curious, I think watching them from afar at least once would be a unique experience. Let's get back to the airport. One peculiar thing about Chinese airports is that when you enter, they gather everyone in one group and block entry, then let them all in at once. So, don't panic; it's best to just wait and then come in. I also waited and entered the airport all at once. Wow , but there aren't even any decent restaurants here. I can't see very well. The airport is huge, but it feels somewhat ambiguously large. I think I'll need to check in and look around a bit more . Okay, then, I'll head to check in. Korean Air handles check-in at Counter B. They operate a total of eight check-in counters: two SKY PRIORITY counters, two Morning Calm counters, and four general counters. Since I have Elite Plus status here, I completed my check-in at the red SKY PRIORITY counter and checked in one piece of luggage. It was a small case, but I was touched that they attached a "Fragile" tag to it. I received a physical boarding pass, not a receipt, along with a lounge pass. I thought it was just an information sheet, but when I got to the lounge, they just took it away. They also checked to make sure the aircraft was arriving safely. My previous flight was so eventful... Since there doesn't seem to be much to see at the airport, I'll go straight through security and head inside. Security checks in China tend to be quite strict. They really scrutinize you thoroughly during the body search, so don't panic; just think of it as China's guidelines. I managed to get into the security area relatively quickly, so I’ll take a quick look around the duty-free shops. There are vending machines near the Chinese liquors, and a Starbucks is located here as well. Aside from that, there isn't much else worth seeing, so I’ll just skip through it and head to the lounge. As a SkyTeam Elite Plus member, I ’ve come to the lounge provided by Korean Air. It is the Air China First & Business Lounge. Although Korean Air is a SkyTeam member, it seems they are using this location because there aren't many suitable lounges at capital airports. If you look here, you can see that Air Koryo also uses this lounge . Okay, so I’ll settle down in this not-so-large lounge and show you the food first. The hot food is prepared with vegetables, mushrooms, sausages, fried eggs, boiled eggs, rice, donuts, and various kinds of porridge . True to a Chinese lounge, dim sum and steamed buns were also available. Wow, that’s a relief. Fruit, bread, and cake are also provided. There is also a dumpling soup live station; you order, they give you a bell, and you pick it up. There are snacks, which are a must-have in a Chinese lounge, as well as beverages and wine. The selection is pretty decent for a Chinese lounge, but this is a lounge provided by Korean Air. Considering the circumstances, it is a bit disappointing. Of course, if you go to places like Kumamoto or Okayama in Japan (I wish for the speedy recovery of the Kumamoto region), there are lounges that only serve tea, but I was still glad that this dumpling soup was delicious. I had a bit of a cold and struggled throughout the journey, but thanks to the dumpling soup, I was able to make it back to Korea alive. This concludes my revenge meal for yesterday evening's China Eastern Airlines in-flight meal. I brought a few snacks to eat, making sure to pick only from reputable brands. The restrooms are plastered with the kinds of things you would see if you flew with Air China. After feeling a bit under the weather in the lounge for a while, I’ll head out in time for boarding. On my way to the gate, I’ll talk briefly about the ticketing machine and the aircraft today. I’m flying on an A321neo today. Korean Air used to be a huge Boeing fan. No, no... they were actually huge Airbus fan. For a while, they kept bringing in Boeing 737s and things like that, but then suddenly, at some point, they started introducing the A321 and A350. I originally booked a business class ticket. This plane is equipped with the Prestige Sleeper 2.0 Product, and I really wanted to try Sleeper 2.0... I tried to book it using Delta mileage, but while it only takes 15,000 miles for Japan, it basically costs 30,000 miles for China... (What kind of standard is that, really?) Does that mean 40,000 miles would allow me to fly business class for about 7 hours? I felt like this wasn't quite right, so since booking with a Skying partner through Delta allows for free cancellation, I canceled and booked an economy ticket instead. There really isn't much to it now that I've come this far... (but I still wanted to fly business class), so I tried to book with Asiana. However, when I tried to book a business class ticket, it was 100,000 won for 20,000 miles, so I thought that wasn't right either. I have arrived in front of Gate 11, where I will be boarding today, and I am at the gate... I was told that boarding would begin as soon as I arrived, so I lined up at SKY PRIORITY. As I entered ahead of the business class passengers, let me briefly explain today's flight. It is Flight KE 2052; the schedule is to take off from PEK at 11:45 AM, fly for two hours, and land at GMP at 2:45 PM. Today, we will be flying on Korean Air's A321neo. The registration number is HL 8557 —a two-year-old aircraft that still wears the old livery. As for the weather today, it snowed quite a bit in Beijing, so we will need to be careful during takeoff and taxiing. That was a brief explanation of the flight; a flight attendant scanned my ticket at the front, and I was able to enter. First of all, you can see the 2-2 seating arrangement with full-flat business class seats. I will try to leave a review of this soon. Although it is a relatively new aircraft, since it is a bit older now, you can see the headrests folded down. Of course, the headrests fold down well. As you continue straight in, my seat today is 54A, a window seat. Since it is a window seat, I went to the restroom first. Since it is a narrow-body restroom, it is bound to be small, but it felt like they made it larger than a 737. I will return to my seat after admiring the view from behind. Personally, I think this seat is the best among Korean Air's economy seats . Let me show you why. First, this monitor ... it is insane. It is a 13.3-inch monitor that reflects a lot of light . I want to show you various things, but the reflection is too intense and I look a mess, so I will just show you the airshow briefly. Just watching the airshow, you can understand why it is the best monitor; the picture quality is that good. Above the monitor, you can see the air vents and reading lights are well-mounted, and below the monitor, there is a slow USB-A type port. However , there are fast charging ports and Type-C ports under the seat, so it would be good to charge your devices there. The seat pitch is enough for a passport to move back and forth vertically, and the seat width is a bit awkward for a passport vertically , but wide enough to move around horizontally. According to the specs, they are 31-32 inches (I guess I felt it was as wide as 32-33 inches ㅠ) and 17.8 inches, respectively. Narrow-body seats are usually in the low 17-inch range. Compared to the 787, which is in the low 17-inch range, this is angelic. The tray table is this one-piece table, and underneath it are the duty-free catalog, the Morning Calm in-flight magazine , and the safety card. Speaking of which, let me verify the aircraft type: A321-200. There are buttons next to the seat, so you can recline it easily, and you can also open and close the window visible on the opposite side. Oh, there was a coat hanger too . Just as I finished taking pictures of everything, the flight attendant came over to greet me and confirm my special in-flight meal. If you fly with SkyTeam Elite Plus status, you always receive a greeting; ah, it feels a bit overwhelming when there is a greeting, but it feels empty without it... honestly, there is a bit of that feeling . (In- flight announcement ) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) (In-flight announcement) They also made the in-flight announcements, and then started playing the safety video in order. Ah, I think I've memorized the Korean Air safety video by now . Still, since there are parts of the announcements that differ by aircraft type, finding those parts is part of the fun. While watching the safety video, the aircraft began pushback, and it looks like there is a slight delay today. I can see a KLM aircraft outside the window . The KLM "Blue Mackerel" looks exactly like Korean Air's new livery. Alright then, I will observe the aircraft heading to the runway both out the window and on the monitor as we take off for today's flight. We have reached cruising altitude; even though it is a short flight, I brought slippers, so I changed into these. The 321 monitor has really severe glare. I hear that they have recently been applying anti-reflective film to monitors starting with the 787-10, but this really needs to be implemented urgently. Honestly, whenever a black screen appears while they are playing things like airshows, I have to face it directly. This is a bit overwhelming. Anyway, I just had the airshow playing and worked on my script for a bit; after a few minutes, the in-flight meal came out right away. Since I requested a special Kosher meal today, it came out quickly. It was a green Kosher meal box. Personally, I tend to prefer Korean Air's Kosher meals for short-hauls , seafood meals for medium-hauls, and standard or gluten-free meals for long-hauls. Anyway, regarding the Kosher meal, although I am not Jewish, I eat it often because it is tasty. They tore open just the middle part like that and heated it up for me. Today 's Kosher meal consisted of something that looked like a fish fillet, chickpeas , a chocolate cake, a piece of fruit bread , and a chocolate roll . The fish fillet-like thing in the center wasn't bad. However, something about it —the seasoning and everything —was missing, about 20%. Eating it with the chickpeas, it really felt like I was just filling my stomach. I looked around and saw there was ketchup , so I quickly drizzled some on it. With the ketchup, the seasoning was actually pretty good. I don't dislike chickpeas, so I forced myself to finish this meal . I regretted it . Oh, and I had dumpling soup at the lounge... I should have just eaten the plate. Still, that chocolate roll was really delicious. The fruits and the chocolate dessert were tasty too. It seems like they really take the desserts seriously with the Kosher meal. I don't think the desserts on the Kosher meal have ever disappointed me. Ever since I hit the peak of short-haul Kosher meals at Narita , I haven't been able to stop eating them... I even had salmon as a Kosher meal again a few days ago, so it would be great if I could choose the Kosher meal option (Delta allows it). Ah, but anyway, for short-haul flights, the Kosher meal is better than the regular in-flight meal. I grumbled a lot, but compared to the meal next to me, the composition was substantial and I filled my stomach pretty well. I definitely filled my stomach... Since there is quite a difference between the highs and lows of Korean Air's short-haul Kosher meals, I'm debating what to do going forward. Maybe I should try the short-haul seafood meal. As I finished my meal, we were passing over Weihai. Even though I had loaded up on sugar, they gave me another can of guava juice. They saw how delicious it was and just gave it to me straight from the can. It was so nice. With this, I think I'll have a pretty intense blood sugar spike. Since Korean Air is known for its great playlists, I put on a playlist to listen to some music. The playlist chosen by me today is this one. Because this is the route from Beijing to Gimpo , we are flying along a path where you can see downtown Seoul and Gimpo clearly. They say you can even see Lotte Tower if you fly Gimpo. The seats are spacious for a narrow-body plane, the seat condition is comfortable, and the monitors are good, so if I were to fly a narrow-body on Korean Air, I would only want to fly this one. I think I need to give the in-flight meal a little more thought. Next time, I should try ordering something different on a short-haul flight. Lastly, it is too early to evaluate the entire airport based only on seeing the Korean Air terminal at Beijing Capital Airport , but there were a few aspects that left something to be desired for a capital airport. Personally, I think Pudong or Guangzhou had slightly better aspects. Even considering it as a typical Chinese airport, it felt pretty similar to Beijing. Personally, next time I’d like to try flying from Daxing and compare the two. reviews.transcript_full: The buzz this year has all been about Riyadh Air, probably the hottest airline launch of the decade. But while they're still finding their feet, could Saudia be upping their game? And has Saudia solved the need for a call button? With essentially the same seat you'll find on British Airways, why did I like this one more? I'll show you tonight, flying their business class from Jeddah to Singapore on a 787, along with a peek inside their flagship lounges. Welcome to King Abdulaziz International. If you're new here, I'm Faz. I've been reviewing airlines since I was a teenager, and I pay for every flight I review, so you get an honest, come-as-you-are view. Jeddah is the main gateway for Hajj pilgrims, but tonight, I'm just connecting. Yep. This terminal's only been open since 2018, and it's more modern than I expected. The layout reminds me of Abu Dhabi's new terminal, just with three piers instead of four. No major European airline flies here now. BA suspended service this year, though Wizz Air has a small base. The Al Fursan lounge sits on the upper floor, and it makes an entrance befitting a flagship. There are even lounges outside for the checking queue, not that anyone needed them at 8:00 p.m. Inside, it's sprawling. A games room and prayer rooms right at the entrance, then a bridge into the main space. The first room is circular, a grand piano at the center, plush leather seating wrapped around it, and a resident robot with drinks if you're too lazy to get your own. Further in, there's a semi-private slumber area, similar to Qatar's Al Mourjan, just scaled down, though I wish it had proper curtains. Past that, more seating, a kids room, the dining area, and a quieter zone at the back. The whole lounge had a relaxed atmosphere, except the buffet, which was as loud as you'd expect. There's a fresh bread counter worth grabbing a roll from. And the buffet itself was solid, but unremarkable. Biryani, chicken tikka, lamb, even pizza and mac and cheese. I kept it light. The food was good, but the real winner was the um Ali, an Egyptian bread pudding. There are several shower suites available here. However, when I went to one, there was no hot water. Staff were on it, but I didn't have an hour to wait. So, they kindly escorted me over to the first class shower rooms instead. Quick look here, slightly calmer. The big difference is ala carte dining. Saudia only has first class on a handful of 777s, hence the empty lounge. The next London flight leaves at 2:30 a.m. The shower rooms themselves were well kitted out with all amenities provided. Afterwards, I had about 30 minutes to enjoy a drink, browse the little library corner, and the duty-free, handy before a flight. Jeddah Airport handles roughly 53 million passengers a year. Big, but easy enough to navigate. Here's our 6-year-old 787-10. Saudia has rebranded in the 2020 and still runs a fleet of 150 plus aircraft. Boarding itself was chaotic, a mix of pilgrims heading home, migrants visiting family, a few Western tourists thrown in. No clear priority lanes, it was a free-for-all. I only got on early through sheer persistence, asking directly when business boarding started. These 787s carry just 24 Collins Aerospace Super Diamond seats, the same shell you'll find on Aeromexico or British Airways. I'm in 4L. 21 in wide, 43-in pitch, 17-in touchscreen with a pillow, bedding, headphones, and water found in each seat. I think I prefer this fit out to BA's version. No storage getting in the way of power points or entertainment console. Storage itself is still generous, split across three levels. I found the boarding music playing in the background quite soothing. Settling in, I was greeted by name and offered hot towels and a welcome drink. I went for the signature date smoothie, which I rather like. Arabic coffee and dates were also on offer, but I did not want anything to interfere with sleep. Headphones weren't true noise canceling, but comfortable enough. Amenity kits were distributed before takeoff. More on those shortly. We pushed back slightly ahead of schedule at 1:00 a.m., nearly full cabin. >> Our flight today would take 8 hours 45 minutes to Singapore. And because of the late departure, the first meal's a lighter one. If you didn't already know, Saudia is a dry airline. But just look at that drinks menu. Going a night without alcohol shouldn't be the deal breaker and an absurd reason not to fly this airline at all. Service started 42 minutes after take off. In the interest of time, I ordered the salmon poke bowl expecting something chilled and quick. I was wrong. 20 minutes later, I was half regretting even ordering wondering if I should have just gone to sleep. By the time it arrived, the salmon was warm, everything else was cold. I finished it in 5 minutes anyway. It was decent, probably an 8 out of 10, but the wait under cut it. Cabin lights were fully dimmed by the time I brushed my teeth. You'll find two business restrooms here, both spotless with some nice amenities. Back at my seat, the mood lighting really stood out against the dark cabin. The amenity kit revealed a rather luxurious offering by Lebanese designer Elie Saab, including all essentials plus face cleanser and moisturizer, hand lotion, lip balm, and a small fragrance to boot. This is easily on par with Qatar's business offering. Another look at the seat, which transforms into a proper flatbed. There was none of that gap issue you find with some BA seats. Even without a mattress pad, I felt properly cozy in it. Now, a new feature I love. reviews.transcript_full:
Cathay Pacific business class has one 
of the best reputations in the sky.   But this regional version is no Aria 
Suite — and might be one of the worst   business class seats I've flown. Today's 
flight takes us from Taipei to Hong Kong,   on the oldest Boeing 777-300 in existence.
Stay tuned for the full review,   and how you can look out and perhaps 
avoid this product for yourself. Our journey begins at Taipei’s main station. I've previously made a full video 
on the in-town check-in service at   Taipei Main Station, which made life so 
much easier — link's in the description.  We were able to complete almost 
the entire check-in process right   at this train station before we took 
the 40 minute train to the airport. My backpack though couldn’t be checked in 
at the train station due to its odd shape.  Cathay has a piece based luggage 
allowance of 2 pieces up to 32kg   each in Business Class. I prefer 
weight based allowances to be honest. Immigration and security were super efficient   and soon we were airside walking 
towards the lounge for the day. Cathay has a huge presence in Taipei So it is no surprise that they operate 
their own lounge at this airport.  The lounge pretty much retains the same 
DNA as Cathays lounges around the world.  First stop, the bar… to get our favourite 
non-alcoholic airline drink - Cathay delight. The centre piece of the lounge is the noodle 
bar offering a good selection of hot dishes   prepared fresh and served minutes later. With our flight almost about to land, 
I headed to our gate to catch a glimpse   of this piece of history. This is 
B-HNE, our aircraft taking us to   Hong Kong today. The cool part? It is 
the original Boeing 777-300 prototype,   the first one ever made and now 28 years old. 
It is impressive that it still flies today. The gate featured cool semiconductor artwork, an 
ode to Taiwan as the leader in global chip supply. Anyway, it is time to board and here is 
a quick look at the seat map for today. Cathay Pacific has a fleet of 
52 Boeing 777 family aircraft,   but 17 of them are the original Boeing 777-300 
non-ER variants. These are a 2 class product with   438 passenger seating. The business class 
consists of 42 seats in a 2-3-2 layout. And, this is it.
As you can see, this is no Aria suite. In fact,   it feels like Cathay’s old Premium economy seat. 
It is a recliner style seat though for its part   comes with decent legroom with three windows. 
It was enough to get this little guy excited. The screen in the distance came 
with a USB socket and there was   an old school power outlet next to the window. In terms of amenities, a pillow and 
paper menus were provided at the seat.   There was a pre-departure drink service and 
soon after that it was time for pushback. (Takeoff roll with pilot commentary) It was a short 1 hour and 15 minute service to 
Hong Kong. Inflight entertainment came in the   form of TV that had to be controlled using a 
remote which was slow and barely responsive.   The entertainment outside was better anyway 
with this view of the Taiwan’s offshore wind   farms appearing to float in the sky.
Despite its age, the aircraft was   equipped with WiFi. And it was 
free for business class passengers. An inflight magazine was available. I 
found the fleet page very interesting   as Cathay lists its future aircraft as 
well as ground service equipment in this. Here is a look at the menu for today’s flight. It 
was pretty impressive for a flight this length.   Two options for main complete with dessert. And 
a decent range of beverages to go with that.   The tray table comes out and here is what the meal   looks like in reality. A proper 
single tray service with proper   crockery and cutlery. The chicken meal 
was served hot and tasted good as well. Here is a quick look at one of 2 lavatories 
serving the business class cabin. All pretty   standard, although this one had a baby change 
table which came in handy. And it was equipped   with Bamford amenities that you will find 
on long haul amenity kits. I've previously   made a full video on Cathay's long-haul 
Business class product. The link's in   the description if you want to see what the 
good version of this experience looks like. Returning back to my seat, it was already time 
for the descent. As Hong Kong came into view,   here are my partying thoughts. Starting with 
the start product, it is top notch and the   Cathay that I have come to love, whether 
it is the meals or the onboard hospitality.  But it is the hard product that is the let down 
here. Only because Asian airlines including Cathay   themselves set such high standards. That said, 
it does come with its warnings. As I mentioned   before there are up to 15 flights per day and 
all I had to do was book an alternative Airbus   A330 or A350 service if I really wanted the 
lie-flat experience. But, hey it is a 2 hour   flight at best and as an aviation nerd, I got 
to experience a piece of aviation history.   What do you think about Cathay’s regional 777 
business class? Let me know in the comments.

reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm trying out ZIPAIR's incredibly cheap business class (ZIP Full Flat). I review both the good and bad points. Please enjoy. Early in the morning, I'm heading to Narita Airport on the first Narita Express. ZIPAIR operates from Narita Airport Terminal 1, so I'm taking this train to Narita Airport Terminal 1 Station. It's around 6 AM now, and I was able to see a beautiful sunrise. If you take the first Narita Express, you'll arrive at Narita Airport Terminal 1 Station at 7:19 AM. I'm heading to the departure lobby on the 4th floor. Terminal 1 is divided into the North Wing and the South Wing, and ZIPAIRs check-in area is in the North Wing. I've arrived at the North Wing on the 4th floor of Terminal 1. ZIPAIR operates flights from Tokyo/Narita to destinations in Asia, North America, and Hawaii. Today's flight departs at 8:55 AM for Manila. The basic fare for business class (ZIP Full Flat) is 55,000 JPY (337 USD). Adding the PREMIUM service package costs an additional 12,500 JPY (76.5 USD). This package includes Prior seat selection, carry-on baggage,  checked baggage, in-flight meal, and an amenity kit. Let's check in. ZIPAIR's check-in counters are C and D. ZIPAIR is a low-cost carrier (LCC) wholly owned by Japan Airlines (JAL). As it's an LCC, you're basically responsible for checking in and dropping off your own baggage. Mobile check-in via smartphone is the standard, but you can also check in using a self-service check-in machine. There's also a priority check-in service called Express Service (for a fee of 3,000 JPY). I won't be using Express Service today. I issued my boarding pass in advance using mobile check-in. Checked baggage is normally subject to a fee, but it's included in this PREMIUM package. I have checked my suitcase, and I will be taking my backpack on board with me. As it's an LCC, you're basically responsible for checking in your own baggage. Normally, you would use the self-service baggage drop-off machine over there. It's 7:42 AM now, and I have about 40 minutes until boarding begins.  I'll go through security and immigration and enter the restricted area. You can use the Narita Premier Lounge for a fee. The fee is 9,200 JPY (56.3 USD). The lounge is 930 square meters in size and has 148 seats. This lounge is uncrowded and offers an excellent selection of alcoholic beverages. You can take off your shoes and relax in a Japanese-style room. You can look out the window at parked airplanes. The seats and tables are spaced far apart, making it very comfortable. There is a buffet area in the center. Bread, desserts, cold meals, sushi, etc. There are four types of hot meals. White rice and soup are also available. There is a beer server and an automatic wine dispenser. Online reviews praise the wide selection of alcoholic beverages. There are various wines and sakes. TWININGS tea and Ito En tea are also available. There are three shower rooms, and amenities such as toothbrushes are provided. You should be able to take a comfortable shower. Now, let's move on to the boarding gate. If you don't go to the lounge, using the restaurants and shops is a good option. There's a McDonald's, and there's a queue in the early morning. It's nice that there's a 7-Eleven in the airport. Starbucks is crowded in the early morning, so I don't feel like using it. My boarding gate is number 21. It's about 7:55 AM now, so I still have plenty of time. My flight to Manila is scheduled for 8:55 AM, a 5-hour and 5-minute flight. The aircraft is a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner. The registration number is JA825J, and it was operated by its parent company JAL from 2012 to 2019, and has been operated by ZIPAIR since January 2020. ZIPAIR uses the Boeing 787 to  efficiently operate medium- and long-haul routes and achieve low fares. There are three reasons for this: long range, excellent fuel efficiency, and the ability to utilize aircraft from its parent company JAL. The exterior of the aircraft is characterized by green lines and the ZIPAIR logo. Green is the corporate color that shows a strong commitment to "safe operation". Boarding begins 30 minutes before departure, at 8:25 AM. All passengers board through the same door. There are two classes: ZIP Full Flat (Business Class) and Standard (Economy Class). Standard (Economy Class) has 272 seats with a 3-3-3 seating arrangement. ZIP Full Flat (Business Class) has 18 seats with a 1-2-1 seating arrangement. The 1-2-1 arrangement is herringbone-style, and all seats have aisle access. There are no doors on the seats. The green headrest covers feature Santa Claus? There is a movable partition between the two center seats. When the partition is closed, you shouldn't be bothered by the person in the next seat. The seats are made of high-quality black genuine leather. There is a luggage rack above each seat. The seat width is 20 inches (51 cm), and the seat pitch is 42 inches (107 cm). The seats recline completely to a full flat position of 180 degrees. My seat is 5A. Headrest. Genuine leather seat, nice to the touch. No personal screen. Reading light. Storage space. Lighting switch, attendant call button. Universal power outlet, USB-A port. A switch to return the seat to its original position. There seems to be a mesh pocket for small items. Seat and lighting control panel. The mesh pocket contains a disposal bag, Boeing 787-8 safety card, and information on in-flight Wi-Fi service. Free internet, in-flight shopping, in-flight entertainment, and flight map. Information on the use of electronic devices on board. Actions that endanger the safety of the aircraft are prohibited by aviation law. Dining table. Can also be used as a laptop desk. There is ample legroom. reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm finally ticking off two things from my aviation bucket list. I'm flying Austrian Airlines's very first scheduled flight from Vienna, Austria to Bond Delgada, Portugal and the beautiful islands of the Assaurus. I've always wanted to visit this incredible destination and I've also always wanted to experience an inaugural flight. When Austrian announced this new route, it felt like the perfect opportunity to take both off my list at once. Today's flight is operated by Austrian Airlines on board an Airbus A320 Neo. With a flight time of around 5 hours and a distance of 3,770 km, this is one of Austrian's longest narrow body routes and certainly one of the most interesting ones. Our route today takes us west across Austria, southern Germany, and Switzerland before continuing over France, Spain, and Portugal and finally across the Atlantic Ocean towards the Aource. Since this flight departs early in the morning, I decided to spend the night at an airport hotel located just across the street from Vienna airport, which makes getting to the terminal incredibly convenient. One thing I really like about Vienna airport is how efficiently everything usually works from baggage drop off to security. I've rarely experienced long waiting times here. As a business class passenger or Star Alliance Gold member, you can simply drop off your baggage at a dedicated check-in counters. Economy class passengers can also use the self-service kiosks and print their baggage tags before heading to the baggage drop. Security at Vienna airport has recently been upgraded with new scanners, meaning you no longer have to remove liquids or electronics from your hand luggage. You're even allowed to bring drinking bottles again with a combined liquid volume of up to 2 L in your carry-on baggage. While making my way towards the gate, I noticed that the airport was very busy today, most likely because the European summer holiday season just had begun. Our flight today departs from gate F5. Since this is Austrian Airlines's inaugural flight to the Azour, there are a few small celebrations before boarding. Passengers could have commemorative photos taken with their own phones while the ground staff also took Polaroid pictures that everyone could keep as a souvenir. It was a nice little touch that immediately made the flight feel a bit more special. Boarding followed the usual Lufansa group priority system starting with home circle members and passengers requiring assistance followed by business class and star alliance gold members before econass passengers were invited to board. >> While boarding every passenger received a commemorative inaugural flight card together with an Austrian Airlines luggage tag. Another nice souvenir from today's flight. Since the aircraft was parked on a remote stand, we boarded one of the airborne buses. Interestingly, this was the first time I had seen a dedicated business class section inside one of Vienna airports buses, which was a pleasant surprise. after a short drive across the apron, our aircraft finally came into view. Today's aircraft with the registration Sulo Oscar is an Airbus A320 Neo delivered new to Austrian Airlines in 2022, making it just under 4 years old. It is currently powered by Pratt and Whitney tuban engines. Although Austrian plans to gradually replace this aircraft with new leap powered A320 news over the coming years. Whenever the weather cooperates, I try remote stand boarding. It gives you a much better opportunity to admire the aircraft and capture some nice photos before stepping on board. My seat today is 1A which is usually my preferred seat whenever I fly on the Airbus A320 family. Like most European airlines, Austrians business class uses standard economycl class seats with the middle seat blocked creating additional personal space. The aircraft features modern Ricaro slimline seats. reviews.transcript_full: South African Airways has been in a struggle spiral for years, a shell of its former self. One step forward, 11 and 1/2 steps back. But even with a downgrade on this trip, my lasting impression was great. So, what actually is going on here? After a beautiful couple of days here in Windhoek, the rain gods caught on to my joy and decided to make my drive to the airport a very wet and a little bit of a treacherous one. The two or three flights, depending on how you count them, in today's video were filmed on two separate days. My ticket is from Windhoek to Abidjan. But that would include an overnight in Johannesburg and then a technical stop in Accra. These triangle routes or technical tag-on legs are very common here in Africa, a way to significantly expand networks without taking a big gamble with capacity. Let me quickly explain my downgrade on this trip. This was a business class ticket. Some months before my flight, I had an itinerary change email sent to me, which I had to accept or reject. I didn't see anything about a downgrade in that email, simply a time change by around 20 minutes. The downgrade I only noticed later, but apparently it was technically part of that email, as I was told by an SAA agent in Johannesburg a couple days prior. It's a short hop from Windhoek. It is what it is, wasn't going to make a big deal out of it. But I was impressed with the check-in agents who themselves insisted on making a big deal of it, in a good way. They explained the downgrade was because of an equipment change to an aircraft without business class, and then they asked me to sit down while they took my passport to the ticket office to get my compensation letter. For anyone booked into business originally, they honored the fare to enter the Paragon Premium Lounge, which was a nice calm space to watch some Netflix. I was very early, not knowing how much extra time the rain was going to add to my drive to the airport. None, apparently. Our flight was scheduled for 6:05 p.m. and we began boarding at 5:23, eventually pushing back at 5:47. Interesting thing though, we departed early without two passengers. Savage timekeeping, and I kind of like it. Luckily, the heavy rain stopped just before we walked out to the plane. If you're enjoying the video and would like to support the channel, there are many ways that you could do so. A quick like on the video and subscribe helps with the algorithm, or you could check out my Patreon, linked in the description below. On Patreon, I post everything from early access or Patreon only videos, newsletters, my best tips and tricks to save money on travel, glimpses behind the scenes, detailed advance itinerary maps, and much, much more. Think of it as a toolbox to save money on or simply improve your next trip, especially if it's to Southeast Asia. If you have questions about upcoming travel, I can help with that, too. Whatever you do though, thanks very much for doing it. >> Hello. >> Inside was a super standard 3 by 3 slimline configuration. I had the whole row to myself, which frankly, I'd prefer over a recliner in a full business class cabin. There is something about African light. It's almost like they have their own saturation hour before golden hour, when everything just looks better. >> [music] [music] [music] [music] >> I reviewed South African Airways a few years ago from Johannesburg to Cape Town, and I actually loved the experience. I remember specifically the meal on board was top-notch a short domestic flight in economy. I also remember saying at the time, early on in their restructuring efforts, if they expand cautiously throughout the African continent and don't touch the long-haul vanity routes that they used to indulge in for 5 years or so, I think their turnaround would be a good one. Well, they launched service to Sao Paulo and Perth like 12 seconds after that video came out. So much for that. Their short flight catering definitely has gone downhill. I raved about the full hot meal last time. This time we had a small chicken snack wrap and a bag of mixed dried fruit. I don't know. Maybe this is what's to be expected on a flight like this and last time they just over delivered. At least there was a free flow of wine. For entertainment, there's streaming available. >> Wow. Wow. Wow. >> And good morning. As I head through security towards the South African lounge, let's talk about South Africa. South African Airways has one of those histories that feels almost too layered to summarize cleanly. Founded in 1934 after the government absorbed Union Airways, SAA grew alongside the country itself, sometimes as a symbol of national pride, other times as a reflection of its political isolation. During the apartheid years, sanctions forced the airline into creative and often inconvenient routing, skirting restricted airspace and turning relatively simple flights into long-haul marathons. When apartheid ended, SAA suddenly had the world back at its doorstep, and for a while it acted like it intended to use all of it. The lounge here is split into two sides, similar to what Singapore Airlines and Lufthansa did. One side is for business class, and the other is for South African elite flyers. The business class side is larger, but more crowded. There's a decent selection of food on offer, and plenty of other quiet secluded spaces closer to the restrooms. Plus, they've got great views of the apron. For a time in the late '90s and early 2000s, SAA was genuinely competitive. It built a long-haul network, joined Star Alliance in 2006 and positioned Johannesburg and sometimes Cape Town as hubs linking Africa to Europe, Asia, and the Americas. They started flying to Miami from Cape Town in 1992 and at the time had the record for the longest two routes on Earth, Johannesburg to New York and second, Cape Town to Miami. Then came the turbulence and not the kind that you can blame on weather. Years of political interference, questionable procurement decisions, and a revolving door of leadership dragged the airline into financial distress. By 2019, it had entered business rescue and for a moment it looked like the curtain might finally close for SAA. Instead, South African reemerged in a smaller, somewhat humbler form. Today, it's owned by the South African government. Though there have been ongoing attempts to partially privatize it through a strategic equity partner. The airline that once spanned continents now operates a very trimmed-down network, primarily focusing on key African routes and a handful of intercontinental services. It's less global powerhouse and more selectively rebuilding, which is probably the only viable approach at this point. And that is reflected in their small fleet, relatively speaking. Gone are the sprawling wide-body operations of the past. Today's lineup is tight. A320 family aircraft handle regional and domestic routes, while a few, just four, Airbus A330s and A340s cover long haul duties. reviews.transcript_full: Today I'm reviewing Qatar Airways Economy Class on a 6 hour flight from London to Doha and since they've been rated the best airline in the world for the last 5 out of 6 years by Skytrax I thought it time to put them to the test and see if Qatar Airways are really as good as people say... and spoiler alert, this was an excellent flight with only a few conceivable issues so sit back and enjoy the ride... and Starting off at London Heathrow Terminal 4 we actually encounter pretty much the only bad thing about the whole experience The check-in queue was long, taking just over 30 minutes to clear to be fair, this was probably our fault as we only arrived 1.5 hours before departure But just bear in mind the queues can be long and plan to arrive at the airport at least 2 hours before departure and you should be fine anyway, we dropped off our bags just 5 minutes before check-in closed and security was much quicker plus they have those new scanners that don't require removing laptops and liquids So we basically walked right through Our gate today was gate 2 right here, a 2 min walk from security whilst in the past I've had gate 25 over here, which is a 10 or 15 min walk and boarding started pretty much as soon as we arrived, so besides the slow check-in everything else was very smooth I couldn't get a good view of the plane from the gate, so in its stead, here's a great view of another random 777-300ER I saw after landing in Doha same aircraft type but different registration whilst waiting for our boarding group I also got a bit of plane spotting in Here's a Qatar A380 also heading to Doha just half an hour before our flight they do up to 10 flights a day between Heathrow & Doha so you'll pretty much always see at least one of their planes here Also there was a Malaysia Airlines A350 about to head to Kuala Lumpur I flew that 2 years ago and it became my most viewed video ever, so shameless plug for people to watch that too... and I think they're a severely underrated airline btw with some of the best food I've had (in Economy at least) Now before we step on board here are the stats and route map for today's flight where we would fly over Europe, Turkey and Iraq before landing into Doha almost 20 minutes early on what would be a very smooth and uneventful flight also random fact, the day we flew the temperature in Doha was 43 degrees, so I was glad we didn't have a bus gate stepping on board we were greeted by some smiley cabin crew and headed to our seats, 21A & B and we paid £50 each for  what QR call "Preferred Seats" near the front of the cabin Only reason I did that is because we had a 2 hour transfer and I wanted to ensure we got off the plane quickly in case of any delays, as you can see from the seat map they have 3 separate Economy cabins but as it happened we were early anyway so it didn't matter Now looking at the seat, it's really good with excellent legroom and it's very well cushioned making it perfect for long haul flights The seatback pocket has 3 separate pouches to that's handy and I also found the seats are very tall which gives quite good privacy for Economy Class also part of the reason I chose this seat was for the great engine view... Back to the seat, you get a folding tray table and USB port, and for some reason an ethernet port... so leave a comment if you have any idea what that could be used for There's a power socket under the seat  Then your bog standard fleece blanket and relatively well sized pillow and I guess I appreciate they provide both on a 6 hour daytime flight as I've flown some airlines who wouldn't on a flight this length and the last feature of the seat is this adjustable headrest Headphones are decent for Economy Class, and I find them better than the in ear headphones many airlines provide and they even give you a little hand wipe, something many airlines don't bother with these days... Then last thing about the seat is the entertainment system and this plane is actually one of Qatar Airways' older cabin so the screen looks a bit dated But the screen itself was fine and has the same slick interface you see on all their aircraft It was also a decent size at 10.6" Which isn't as good as the 13" screens you get in Emirates Economy for example but it is comparable to most major airlines The movie and tv selection was extensive so no complaints there the only thing that confused me is the map seemed to be stuck in Arabic and I couldn't find a way to change it and this only affected the map, everything else was in English... Also they have this slightly dated tv remote which I personally never use but I guess it's there if you want it And lastly before the safety video, it has this good picture in picture function So you can watch a movie whilst having the map in a smaller window, or vice versa Now here is the Muslim travel prayer and safety video, featuring Kevin Hart... and just on the safety video, they say they don't want it to be "no nonsense that is a direct call out to Emirates who say at the start of their safety video how no nonsense it is... so Qatar's video is definitely a bit more interesting than Emirates, but still not the world's greatest like they say Also spotted this weird wingless and tail-less plane, so leave a comment if you know that it is... Now it's time for the takeoff, where we got a great view of all the planes parked at London Heathrow... even if the weather was a little grey Service started with a drink and a bag of crunchy corn snacks I got a ginger ale to drink and then I also asked for coffee and they made me some actually impressive as most airlines would just tell you they only serve coffee after the main meal so props to Qatar Airways for being very accomodating there Then for the main meal it was a choice of beef or vegetarian pasta and I got the beef Now presentation and portion-wise this was great However, taste-wise it was one of the blandest meals I can remember having on a plane... not bad... just bland so a bit more flavour or maybe some salt and pepper would pouches would be nice you do get metal cutlery though, which is a plus and also a first for me on a plane, foccacia bread, though it was a bit stodgy This was Spätzle by the way (German pasta) Then after the main meal hot drinks and Biscoff were served And now for the loo review, it was kept clean... but that's about it just a normal airplane toilet otherwise though it did have a lot of mirrors... Another very strong point for this flight was the free superfast Starlink Wifi It worked flawlessly, was super fast and they also let you watch live sport if you use a QR code on the screen It was fast enough to watch Youtube videos in 1080p with no issue and so far they've just rolled out Starlink to almost all of their Boeing 777s and some Airbus A350s  but eventually it will come to all Qatar Airways Aircraft, though the wait might be long... and very lastly before landing we were served a light snack with a choice of chicken or vegetarian pastry And I have to say, this Harissa Chicken roll was better than a Greggs sausage roll as sacriligeous as that may be to say to my UK viewers Coming in to land we got a view of these crazy private mansions, each one on its own private island though I have to say, if I paid that much money for a private island I might get a bit annoyed by the sound of planes constantly flying over So here we are in Doha, where the outside temperature was 43 degrees at the time of arrival and I'm happy to report it was a very good flight Only just over 6 hours so you could barely class it as long haul but they did get 2 meal services in and the crew were really good throughout so I would happily book Qatar Airways on a proper long haul flight in the future and between today's flight and the connecting flight I took with them in Business Class I think Qatar Airways are probably now my favourite Middle Eastern Airline, Just slightly beating Emirates and Etihad Though I'm flying Etihad next month from London to Singapore and back so we'll see if they can get some redemption there... and I've made a bid to upgrade to Business on one of those flights so hopefully it comes through and very lastly, I was connecting onwards to Ho Chi Minh City after this and the last time I transferred at Doha we had to go through a security check so I was pleasantly surprised when we walked off the plane straight into the terminal anyway, that meant our 2 hour layover was more than enough time and we had a good chance to explore the airport especially this cool rainforest area... now without further ado, here is my final score for Qatar Airways Economy Really my only gripe with the entire experience was how bland the main meal was but literally everything else was well above average so I can forgive them for that  definitely earning their rank as one of the world's best airlines... reviews.transcript_full: We're at Warsaw Chopin Airport. Ahead of us is an Airbus A330-300 in Qatar Airways livery. The aircraft that will take us to Doha, Qatar, today. This model is a wide-body, long-haul aircraft used on intercontinental routes. In this configuration, there are nearly 300 seats divided into two classes: business and economy. The A330-300 has two aisles, so even when fully booked, moving around the cabin isn't particularly troublesome. Qatar Airways uses these aircraft primarily on medium- and long-haul routes, such as the one from Warsaw to Doha, which takes about 5.5 hours. In this episode, we'll focus on Economy Class. We'll show you exactly what awaits you on board, the service, the entertainment system, and, of course, the flight itself. We start with a classic: boarding, a quick glance at the interior, and we find our seat. The seats are arranged in a 2-4-2 configuration with a standard pitch. Before the plane takes off, crew hands out wet wipes. Hands can be sanitized. Each seat has a hanger, a paper safety manual, an in-flight entertainment screen, a headset, headphones, a blanket, a pillow, and a drink holder. There's also a fold-out table, which we'll use for a meal in a moment. The Oryx One in-flight entertainment system awaits us on the screen. Qatar Airways offers a wide selection of movies, TV series, music, and games. A special feature is the section dedicated to our destination, Doha. Here, you can read about local attractions, history, culture, and what's worth seeing after landing. Before takeoff, you can watch a Qatar Airways safety video, as usual . It's quite creatively presented. Let's see what else you can watch in the movies section. There are new releases, as well as classics and productions from various countries. There are also games ranging from simple puzzles to classic arcade games. For the little ones, there's a separate section with animated films. Time for lunch. The flight attendant hands out a tray with a meal. We're served chicken with rice and vegetables. A small bottle of water, dessert, and, unusually in economy class, metal cutlery. The whole thing looks aesthetically pleasing and, considering the on-board conditions, quite tasty. The restrooms are also clean. There are air freshener sprays, running water, and paper towels. It's all the usual fare, but it's really well-maintained, and the restrooms are indeed spotless. A promotional video for Qatar plays on the screens before landing. A few shots of museums, the desert, stadiums, and seaside bars. A mini-guide that might inspire you to plan your sightseeing. After landing and taxiing, it's time to disembark. Standard procedure: first business class, then economy. A final glance at the cabin, and we're off to the terminals in Doha. This is what our flight from Warsaw to Doha with Qatar Airways looked like on an Airbass A330-300. If you have any questions about the flight or the route itself, let me know in the comments. If you'd like more flight and travel vlogs, subscribe and give me a thumbs up. See you in the next episode.

reviews.transcript_full: The 2026Qar Airways Airbus A380 is more than just an aircraft. It is an experience that combines scale, comfort, and elegance in a way that only the largest passenger jet in the world can deliver. For years, the Airbus A380 has symbolized longhaul luxury. And Qatar Airways has embraced it fully by refining every detail to create a journey that feels closer to a five-star hotel in the sky than conventional air travel. From the moment you step inside the aircraft, the first thing you notice is the sense of space. The double-deck design means high ceilings, wide aisles, and cabins that feel open and welcoming. Qatar Airways has redesigned the interiors for 2026 with modern lighting, upgraded climate controls, and materials chosen to create a calm atmosphere. Even on flights lasting over 14 hours, passengers feel comfortable and refreshed. Economy class has been enhanced with better seat ergonomics, improved leg room, and larger personal entertainment screens. Each seat now includes charging ports, USBC connectivity, and Bluetooth pairing, so passengers can use their own headphones. The entertainment system is faster, more intuitive, and offers thousands of hours of movies, TV shows, music, and games. Even on the longest routes, there is more than enough to keep everyone entertained. Premium economy is now available on the Qatar Airways A380. Positioned as a perfect middle ground. The seats are wider, recline deeper, and offer extra personal space. Passengers in this cabin also enjoy upgraded dining with menus designed specifically for longer flights along with larger entertainment screens and amenities that make the experience feel much more premium without the price tag of business class. Business class remains one of the highlights of flying Qatar Airways. The A380 features the airlines award-winning Quit redesigned for the spacious cabin. Each seat converts into a fully flat bed and is equipped with privacy doors. Couples and families can create private areas by opening partitions, making the cabin flexible for different types of travelers. Dining is on demand with restaurant style service, fine ingredients, and presentation designed to feel like a luxury restaurant above the clouds. Wi-Fi is fast and reliable, allowing passengers to work, stream, or stay connected throughout the journey. First class is where the aircraft truly shines. The 2026 update includes larger private suites, enhanced finishes, and luxury bedding. Each suite offers a flat bed, large highdefinition screen, direct aisle access, and personal storage. The menus feature gourmet dishes designed by top chefs paired with premium wines and champagnes carefully selected for altitude. Exclusive amenity kits, designer sleepwware, and refined service make first class feel like a private retreat in the sky. One of the most unique features of the Qar Airways A380 is the onboard lounge. Located on the upper deck, it serves as a social hub for first and business class passengers. With comfortable seating, a bar offering premium beverages, and a selection of light snacks, the lounge is designed for both relaxation and conversation. The 2026 upgrade introduced softer lighting, quieter surroundings, and improved seating arrangements that encourage interaction or peaceful downtime depending on passenger preferences. Technology also plays a central role in the passenger experience. The Orex 1 entertainment platform now features 4K resolution screens in premium cabins and an interface that responds instantly. Passengers can create playlists that carry over to future flights if they are frequent travelers. Wi-Fi has been upgraded to high-speed satellite systems, making it possible to stream, video call, and work without interruptions. This connectivity transforms the A380 into both a leisure and business environment. Qatar Airways has also made strides in sustainability with its A380 operations. The updated engines have been tuned for better fuel efficiency. Cabin refurbishments use lighter materials, and the airline invests heavily in sustainable aviation fuels and carbon offset programs. For passengers who are conscious about the environment, this commitment adds reassurance that luxury and responsibility can exist together. Cabin crew continued to play a vital role in shaping the journey. Qatar Airways is known for its attentive service, and on the A380, this reputation is enhanced by the generous space and carefully designed service routines. Crew members anticipate passenger needs, assist with dietary requests, and maintain a calm, professional presence that makes every traveler feel valued. Another detail that passengers notice is how quiet the cabin is. Despite the size of the aircraft, sound insulation and engine design make the flight environment peaceful. This is especially important on overnight routes where rest is a priority. The improved air quality systems also reduce fatigue, making longhaul travel less exhausting than on smaller aircraft. Families are well cared for on board. Qatar Airways provides children's entertainment content, kid-friendly meals, and practical support like bassinets and early boarding. The spacious cabins make traveling with children more manageable, and parents appreciate the extra consideration that helps keep younger passengers comfortable and entertained. The A380 is deployed on some of Qar Airways most important routes. Cities like London, Paris, Sydney, and Bangkok see the aircraft regularly, reflecting demand for both capacity and premium service. These are high-profile routes where the airline showcases its flagship product, ensuring that passengers experience the very best the brand has to offer. For aviation enthusiasts, the A380 is still an incredible sight with its massive wingspan and double-deck design that towers over most other aircraft at the airport. Boarding this aircraft always feels like a special occasion. And Qatar Airways has leaned into that sense of wonder by making the onboard experience as memorable as possible. Every detail from the seats and dining to the entertainment and service is designed to make passengers feel that they are part of something extraordinary. The 2026Qar Airways Airbus A380 is more than just a means of travel. It is a statement about what air travel can be. It blends tradition with modernity, combining the scale of the world's largest passenger aircraft with the elegance and service that have made Qar Airways one of the most respected airlines in the world. Whether flying in economy, business, or first, the journey offers comfort, technology, and hospitality that elevate longhaul travel into a truly remarkable experience. Thanks for watching.

reviews.transcript_excerpt: The 15-in touchscreen is bright and…

captions.text: The 15-in touchscreen is bright and

reviews.transcript_full: Hello everyone. Welcome back to our channel. Today, we're taking you along on our journey flying ANA Premium Economy departing from Vancouver International Airport to Tokyo Haneda. We'll also share our experience at the Plaza Premium Lounge. Our trip actually started in Seattle. We drove about 2 hours to Vancouver. This is one of our favorite travel hacks. Flying from Vancouver to Japan is usually 20-30% cheaper than flying from Seattle. We parked our car at Vancouver Airport's long-term valet parking, which cost us about $200 for 4 weeks, significantly cheaper than parking at SeaTac. For this flight, we paid $826 USD per person one way from Vancouver compared to about $1,182 USD from Seattle. Quite a big difference. With Premium Economy, you were allowed two 23 kg checked bags each. Since we had five bags, we paid an additional $150 baggage fee. After check-in, security was quick and smooth. We made our way into the international terminal, explored some duty-free shops, and then headed to the Plaza Premium Lounge near gate D67. The lounge was clean and not too busy when we arrived, but it's definitely on the smaller side. I can imagine it getting quite crowded during peak hours. >> Soup options included tomato soup and chicken soup. Pork ribs and maple chicken. Grilled vegetables and fried potatoes. Salads and desserts. There are not a lot of options for food selections. For drink, there is a coffee machines for lattes and cappuccinos. Canadian wines from Okanagan Valley and Niagara Peninsula. A few basic spirits like Bacardi rum and Canadian whiskey. And of course local lager and pale ale beers. We grabbed a glass of wine and some snacks and just sat back for a bit. Overall, the lounge is functional, but not memorable. It's a decent place to relax, but don't expect a luxury experience. After 30 minutes, we headed to our gate, which was just a few minutes walk from the lounge. Hi, hi. So, we are flying from Vancouver to Tokyo. We stay in Tokyo for 4 days. We will enjoy it. Shop to lot of shopping in Tokyo. Then, we will fly to stop by Korea for 10 hours. And then, Mongolia. Soon, it was time to board our flight, a Boeing 787. Walking into the premium economy cabin, the layout is a 2-3-2 configuration, creating a more spacious feel compared to standard economy. However, our first impression of the seats was slightly mixed. While the space itself is generous, the seats did feel a bit worn and dated, especially compared to JAL's newer cabins. One thing we noticed, compared to JAL, ANA's premium economy seats do not include a privacy divider between seats. On JAL, that divider gives you a bit of personal space helpful when you're sitting next to someone you don't know. The amenity kit is simple and functional. You get slippers, eye mask, toothbrush, basic headphones, but to be honest, compared to JAL, the amenities feel a step below. JAL offers more thoughtful touches like their heated eye mask, which really enhances comfort on long flights. And also, it comes with a bag. With ANA, everything is there, but it feels more basic and minimal rather than premium. You get a 38-in seat pitch, giving you significantly more legroom, a recline function with leg rest, which really helps on long-haul flights, a wide seat design, making it easier to relax without feeling cramped. The 15-in touchscreen is bright and responsive, and there's also a universal power outlet, USB charging port, personal reading light. Overall, while the seat design isn't the most modern, it still delivers a comfortable and practical premium economy experience. ANA provides noise-canceling Panasonic-branded headphones, which is a nice touch in terms of branding, but in terms of comfort, we found them just okay. After wearing them for a longer period, they started to feel a bit uncomfortable around the ears. Shortly after takeoff, we were served a welcome drink including champagne along with a small snack of rice crackers. ANA offers a wide range of beverages including wine, sake, and shochu, whiskey, gin, and vodka, beer, and even non-alcoholic beer. One nice touch, the shochu is served in a small individual bottle. For the main meal, we had several options. Minced pork sauce over steamed rice, seafood turmeric rice, ANA's original chicken cutlet curry. We chose the minced pork dish. The meal was arranged with smoked salmon macaroni salad, fried potatoes with shiso, cheese crackers, and a small dessert gelato. The flavors were balanced, not fancy, but satisfying. After the meal, we enjoyed some matcha tea with a milk biscuit. Japanese snacks and baked goods just hit differently. Simple, but incredibly well done. Throughout the flight, there were also light snack options available including instant noodles. On long-haul flights like this, one of the biggest challenges is staying comfortable and avoiding inflammation. We always fly with the Hyperice Normatec Legs Compression System and Firefly devices. It's a portable leg compression device designed to improve circulation and reduce swelling, which is helpful when you're sitting for more than 4 hours flight. About midway through the flight, she put it on and it helped increase blood flow circulation and reduce inflammation. The device gently inflates and deflates in cycles, applying pressure from the feet upward, almost like a massage for your legs. We already have reviews for these devices and feel welcome to watch it in our channel. Now, let's check out the lavatories. As expected from a Japanese airline, the bathrooms were consistently clean throughout the flight, something ANA does very well. A standout feature is the bidet function, which adds an extra level of comfort and hygiene. However, one limitation, premium economy passengers cannot access business class lavatories, so you'll be using the shared economy section. That said, they were well maintained and never felt overly crowded during our flight. In between meals, ANA also offers light snack options, which is always a nice touch on a long-haul flight. One of the highlights was their instant noodles, and they actually offered two options, a vegetarian version and a regular version. We tried both and they were delicious. About an hour before landing, we were served a light meal box with a small sandwich, yogurt, apple slices. It was fresh and clean, but compared to JAL, it felt slightly less premium and less memorable. Overall, ANA premium economy feels like a more simplified version of JAL's premium economy experience, especially when it comes to service details, food, and overall comfort. That doesn't mean it's bad. In fact, it still offers a comfortable seat, solid in-flight service, and a reliable long-haul experience. But when you compare it side by side with JAL, you start to notice the differences in the finer details, things like seat privacy, amenities, and dining quality. Those small touches are where JAL really stands out. So, I'd say ANA delivers a good and dependable premium economy product, but there is definitely room for improvement to reach that next level. After landing, we made our way through immigration, which was smooth, by the way, and then headed to baggage claim. And this is where something really stood out. Watching how luggage is handled in Japan is impressive. As the bags came out onto the carousel, you could see that they were carefully placed, almost respectfully, rather than just being dropped or tossed. Many of the suitcases were even aligned neatly, handles facing outward, making it easier for passengers to grab them. It might seem like a small detail, but it reflects something bigger. There's a level of care, precision, and respect for people's belongings that you don't always see in other airports. Getting Thank you so much for watching. If you enjoyed this video, please like and subscribe. It really helps support our channel. We have more travel and climbing adventures coming soon, and we can't wait to share them with you. See you in the next adventure.

reviews.transcript_full: Today, I fly ANA's domestic premium class from Tokyo Haneda to Yamaguchi Ube Airport. An incredible seat, excellent [music] food, automatic beer machines, and two aborted landings later, here's my verdict on the All Nippon Airways domestic flight service. Welcome to Tokyo Haneda Airport, where today we are having a beautiful spring day looking across the apron and taxiway of Haneda International Airport. But, we're going for something a little bit different today, and we're not traveling domestically in a train. We are actually taking a ANA All Nippon Airways Airbus A321 premium class service from Tokyo Haneda International Airport all the way down to Yamaguchi Ube Airport. We had a bit of time to kill after arriving on Finnair from Helsinki. Video out very soon. As we headed to the domestic premium check-in area. This flight left from the purely domestic terminal, terminal 2, where we had to check in our luggage after Finnair were not able to check it through for us. I wasn't able to capture much of the check-in process, nor the security, but it was very swift and easy to get through. We then headed into the ANA domestic premium class lounge, which is also available to Star Alliance Gold members. It's not really much to write home about, and I would say Japanese domestic airports are more akin to a bus terminal in the sense that people sort of very much just turn up and go. There's no hot food available, and the food was available was in the form of pre-packaged snacks. Albeit, there was actually a pretty good selection of nuts. And for those who are fancying a beer, you can use one of these excellent automatic machines, which always make me look in wonder. I wouldn't turn up early for this. We then headed from the lounge to head to our departure gate here at Haneda, where our Airbus A321 aircraft was waiting for us. I actually really like the livery of ANA. It looks so modern and sleek despite being around for a long time. Something that really surprised me about this flight, and perhaps Japanese domestic flights in general, was just how how can I say it, chaotic the boarding felt compared to everything else in Japan. It just felt really busy and and not very organized, particularly when you compare to other domestic travel options such as the Shinkansen. It just was not in the same league. However, boarding quickly began, and we headed through the priority boarding into the jet bridge, and it was all quite smooth with very little boarding not boarding as you get at other airports. So, the Japanese domestic travel market is one of the most interesting in the whole of the world, particularly considering the size of this country. So, you have two main domestic airlines in the form of Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways, who I'm flying today. JAL have three classes of service on a lot of their flights, so that is economy, class J, which is sort of a premium economy, and then you have first class. While ANA has just economy and premium class. Uh that means for most travelers, JAL have the better premium class product. However, for me, the flight schedule of the ANA flights to Yamaguchi suited my travel far better. And also, it is just completely illogical that Japan has a domestic flying network at all, considering how excellent the wider train and Shinkansen network is. However, I'm not going to complain on taking these excellent flights within this excellent country. And with that, it was time to see what the premium class had to offer from ANA. And here it is, a 2-2 recliner seat layout in [music] just two rows, making for an extremely exclusive experience with an abundance of legroom to match. This is excellent considering these flights are only serve up to 4 hours. This is extremely flexible winged headrest, which is very comfortable to lay on. And then you also have the recline function, which is electronically controlled, unlike premium economy seats. And it goes back fairly easily, as you can see here, and then provides relatively good support for your legs when in that recline mode. >> [music] >> Despite being such a short 90-minute to hour flight, ANA provides slippers on board and quite a chunk of amenities for all passengers. There's a set of headphones available branded with Panasonic, and also a [music] blanket for you to use. This is actually a rather substantial blanket, and is very good considering that we were visiting in quite a chilly part of the year. Between the seats, there's international power outlet and USB ports. While straight ahead, there is no in-flight entertainment, but plenty of storage for any of your personal possessions. Between the seats, there's these remote controls, and then above there is shared entertainment screens. The in-flight safety video, which at this time featured Pokémon, played on the screens above, and was rather engaging along with a lot of these commercials, which really caught my eye, even though I had no idea what they were for. Apparently a credit card. Wi-Fi is absolutely free of charge for all passengers on domestic ANA flights, which is quite good, and was rather speedy in my experience. It hosts a number of like the in-flight [music] entertainment services that you would expect on a personal screen, such as flight map tracking and some on-demand programming. You're also able to access other internet services on there, not just ANA stuff. >> [music] >> We are now in the air. Let's take a look at the wider in-flight service, and considering this is a short flight, there isn't a ton to go wrong here. >> [music] >> We took a very quick peek at the in bathroom. Very small, not much to see, but the highlight was probably the food and drink offering. Today's meal was a bento box type thing, which was really tasty and full of fresh ingredients. I had There's an extensive selection of sake, shochu, sparkling wine, white wine, red wine, beer, and alcohol-free beer alongside your [music] meal, which is a cold meal, but was extremely tasty. And to finish it off, we had this alongside a bottle of sake. A really nice way to finish off the meal. But then, trouble arose. So, the flight actually was in quite quick succession and went relatively smoothly until we were about to land into Yamaguchi Ube, where we had two aborted landings and were told that we might have to return all the way back to Tokyo. This was not ideal and meant that the flight landed in the end about 2 hours late. Even despite being a season traveler, I was very nervous at this moment. I've never experienced a aborted landing, certainly not two aborted landings. I could see out the window how foggy it was in Yamaguchi, and they just could not land. Um but eventually we did in the end, which caused some issues when we arrived as we couldn't get a taxi, and we almost missed the last train. However, all was well in the end, and we got in fine. So, would I recommend ANA domestic premium class? And in reality, I think I would. It's not a massive cost to upgrade, and while JAL may have a better product, I actually found it very comfortable and a very good option to take within the country. Uh there are some areas where you could perhaps improve it. Um certainly the lounges aren't great, but it's very much a turn up and go service. And also, I would say that perhaps um some uh metal cutlery and also glass glasses would be better than paper cups. But in short, it's the the high standards of service you expect from Japan in the air, and really these short flights, and even up to 3 or 4 hours to the likes of Okinawa, they are absolutely brilliant. I can't wait to get some more experiences traveling domestically in Japan in the future. Now, let's see that moment where we landed into Ube Airport. >> Surprisingly for quite a provincial airport, there was actually jet bridges here and the arrival process was really smooth. The bags came out pretty swiftly and meant that we could actually head out into the main town of Yamaguchi. I hope you enjoyed this video and a very brief look at ANA's domestic premium class. If you'd like to see some other premium Japanese Airlines experiences, please tap the videos in here. Otherwise, thank you so much for watching. See you soon. Bye-bye.
